1 Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. But 12 345✦2as for me, my feet were almost gone. My steps had nearly slipped.6 3 For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.7 ✦4 For there are no struggles in their death, but their strength is firm.8 ✦5 They are free from burdens of men, neither are they plagued like other men.9 ✦6 Therefore pride is like a chain around their neck. Violence covers them like a garment.10 ✦7 Their eyes bulge with fat. Their minds pass the limits of conceit.11 12✦8 They scoff and speak with malice. In arrogance, they threaten oppression.13 ✦9 They have set their mouth in the heavens14. Their tongue walks through the earth15.16 ✦10 Therefore their people return to them, and they drink up waters17 of abundance.18 ✦11 They say, “How does God19 know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?”20 ✦12 Behold, these are the wicked. Being always at ease, they increase in riches.21 ✦13 Surely I have cleansed my heart22 in vain, and washed my hands in innocence,23 ✦1424 ✦15 For all day long I have been plagued, and punished every morning. If I had said, “I will speak thus”, behold, I would have betrayed the generation of your children.25 ✦16 When I tried to understand this, it was too painful for me—26 ✦1727 28✦18 until I entered God’s sanctuary, and considered their latter end. Surely you set them in slippery places. You throw them down to destruction.29 ✦19 How they are suddenly destroyed! They are completely swept away with terrors.30 ✦20 As a dream when one wakes up, so, Lord31, when you awake, you will despise their fantasies.32 33✦21 For my soul was grieved. I was embittered in my heart34.35 22 I was so senseless and ignorant. I was a brute beast before you.36 ✦23 Nevertheless, I am continually with you. You have held my right hand.3738 ✦24 You will guide me with your counsel, and afterward receive me to glory39.4041 ✦25 Whom do I have in heaven42? There is no one on earth43 whom I desire besides you.4445 ✦26 My flesh and my heart46 fails, but God47 is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.484950 ✦27 For, behold, those who are far from you shall perish. A contemplation by Asaph.

1 God1, why have you rejected us forever? Why does your anger smolder against the sheep of your pasture?2 ✦2 Remember your congregation, which you purchased of old, which you have redeemed to be the tribe of your inheritance: Mount Zion, in which you have lived.3 ✦3 Lift up your feet to the perpetual ruins, all the evil that the enemy has done in the sanctuary. 4 Your adversaries have roared in the middle of your assembly. They have set up their standards as signs.4 5 They behaved like men wielding axes, cutting through a thicket of trees.5 6✦6 Now they break all its carved work down with hatchet and hammers.7 7 They have burned your sanctuary to the ground8. They have profaned the dwelling place of your Name.9 8 They said in their heart, “We will crush them completely.” They have burned up all the places in the land10 where God11 was worshiped.12 ✦9 We see no miraculous signs. There is no longer any prophet, neither is there among us anyone who knows how long. ✦10 How long, God13, shall the adversary reproach? Shall the enemy blaspheme your name forever? ✦11 Why do you draw back your hand, even your right hand? Take it from your chest and consume them! ✦12 Yet God14 is my King of old, working salvation15 throughout the earth16. 13 You divided the sea by your strength. You broke the heads of the sea monsters in the waters17.18 ✦14 You broke the heads of Leviathan in pieces. You gave him as food to people and desert creatures.19 ✦15 You opened up spring and stream. You dried up mighty rivers. ✦16 The day is yours, the night is also yours. You have prepared the light20 and the sun.21 ✦17 You have set all the boundaries of the earth22. You have made summer and winter.23 ✦18 Remember this, that the enemy has mocked you, Yahweh. Foolish people have blasphemed your name.2425 26✦19 Don’t deliver the soul27 of your dove to wild beasts. Don’t forget the life of your poor forever.28 ✦20 Honor your covenant29, for haunts of violence fill the dark places of the earth30.31 ✦21 Don’t let the oppressed return ashamed. The tumult of those who rise up against you ascends continually.

Yes, I will obey it with my whole heart54. ✦35 Direct me in the path of your commandments, for I delight in them. ✦36 Turn my heart55 toward your statutes, not toward selfish gain. ✦37 Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.5657 ✦38 Fulfill your promise to your servant, that you may be fear58ed.59 ✦39 Take away my disgrace that I dread, for your ordinances are good60. 6140 Behold, I long for your precepts! Revive me in your righteousness62. VAV

✦41 Let your loving kindness also come to me, Yahweh, your salvation63, according to your word. 64✦42 So I will have an answer for him who reproaches me, for I trust in your word. ✦43 Don’t snatch the word of truth out of my mouth, for I put my hope in your ordinances. 44 So I will obey your law continually, forever and ever. 45 I will walk in liberty, for I have sought your precepts.65 ✦46 I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed. ✦47 I will delight myself in your commandments, because I love them. 48 I reach out my hands for your commandments, which I love. I will meditate on your statutes.

ZAYIN

49 ✦50 Remember your word to your servant, because you gave me hope. This is my comfort in my affliction, for your word has revived me.66 ✦51 The arrogant mock me excessively, but I don’t swerve from your law. 52 I remember your ordinances of old, Yahweh, and have comforted myself. 6753 Indignation has taken hold on me, because of the wicked who forsake your law. 54 Your statutes have been my songs in the house where I live.68 ✦55 I have remembered your name, Yahweh, in the night, and I obey your law. 69✦56 This is my way, that I keep your precepts.

HETH

5770 7158 Yahweh is my portion. I promised to obey your words. I sought your favor with my whole heart72. Be merciful to me according to your word. ✦59 I considered my ways, and turned my steps to your statutes.73 ✦60 I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.74 ✦61 The ropes of the wicked bind me, but I won’t forget your law. ✦62 At midnight I will rise to give thanks to you, because of your righteous75 ordinances. ✦63 I am a friend of all those who fear76 you, of those who observe your precepts.77 ✦64 The earth78 is full of your loving kindness, Yahweh. Teach me your statutes.

TETH

7980✦65 8166 You have treated your servant well, according to your word, Yahweh.

Teach me good82 judgment and knowledge, for I believe in your commandments.83 ✦67 Before I was afflicted, I went astray; but now I observe your word.84 ✦68 You are good85, and do good. Teach me your statutes. ✦69 The proud have smeared a lie upon me. With my whole heart86, I will keep your precepts.87 ✦70 Their heart88 is as callous as the fat, but I delight in your law. 71 It is good89 for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes.9091 ✦72 The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver. ↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BLASPHEMY In the sense of speaking evil of God this word is found in Psalm 74:18; Isaiah 52:5; Romans 2:24; Revelation 13:1, 6; 16:9, 11, 21. It denotes also any kind of calumny, or evil-speaking, or abuse (1 Kings 21:10; Acts 13:45; 18:6, etc.). Our Lord was accused of blasphemy when he claimed to be the Son of God (Matthew 26:65; comp. Matthew 9:3; Mark 2:7). They who deny his Messiahship blaspheme Jesus (Luke 22:65; John 10:36). Blasphemy against the Holy Ghost (Matthew 12:31, 32; Mark 3:28, 29; Luke 12:10) is regarded by some as a continued and obstinate rejection of the gospel, and hence is an unpardonable sin, simply because as long as a sinner remains in unbelief he voluntarily excludes himself from pardon. Others regard the expression as designating the sin of attributing to the power of Satan those miracles which Christ performed, or generally those works which are the result of the Spirit’s agency.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). AHOLAH she has her own tent, a name used by Ezekiel (23:4, 5, 36, 44) as a symbol of the idolatry of the kingdom of Israel. This kingdom is described as a lewdwoman, an adulteress, given up to the abominations and idolatries of the Egyptians and Assyrians. Because of her crimes, she was carried away captive, and ceased to be a kingdom. (Comp. Psalm 78:67-69; 1 Kings 12:25-33; 2 Chronicles 11:13-16.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WAILING-PLACE , JEWS’ a section of the western wall of the temple area, where the Jews assemble every Friday afternoon to bewail their desolate condition (Psalm 79:1, 4, 5). The stones in this part of the wall are of great size, and were placed, as is generally believed, in the position in which they are now found in the time of Solomon. “The congregation at the wailing-place is one of the most solemn gatherings left to the Jewish Church, and as the writer gazed at the motley concourse he experienced a feeling of sorrow that the remnants of the chosen race should be heartlessly thrust outside the sacred enclosure of their fathers’ holy temple by men of an alien race and an alien creed. Many of the elders, seated on the ground, with their backs against the wall, on the west side of the area, and with their faces turned toward the eternal house, read out of their well-thumbed Hebrew books passages from the prophetic writings, such as Isaiah 64:9-12” (King’s Recent Discoveries, etc.). The wailing-place of the Jews, viewed in its past spiritual and historic relations, is indeed “the saddest nook in this vale of tears.” (See LAMENTATIONS, BOOK OF.)

In the psalm quoted above the powers that destroyed the Jewish nation are compared to wild boars and wild beasts of the field.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.19 (c. 350 AD)

'I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High' (LXX 81:6 — egō eipa theoi este kai huioi hypsistou pantes) — Athanasius marks Ps 82:6 as the THEŌSIS-BY-GRACE anchor — explicitly cited by the Word himself at Jn 10:34-35 to silence the blasphemy-charge for his ego eimi self-identification. The human-recipients of the divine-word are called 'gods' by-participation, by-grace, by-econoomic-divine-naming; the Word is God by-nature, by-essence, by-eternal-generation. Athanasius's signature theōsis-formula in DI §54 — 'He was made man that we might be made God' (autos enēnthrōpēsen hina hēmeis theopoiēthōmen) — rests on this Ps 82:6 / Exo 7:1 / 2 Pet 1:4 grammar: gods-by-grace through-the-Word who-is-God-by-nature. The Tewahedo soteriology preserves this asymmetric grammar at every catechetical level.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GEBAL a line (or natural boundary, as a mountain range). (1.) A tract in the land of Edom south of the Dead Sea (Psalm 83:7); now called Djebal. (2.) A Phoenician city, not far from the sea coast, to the north of Beyrout (Ezekiel 27:9); called by the Greeks Byblos. Now Jibeil. Mentioned in the Amarna tablets. An important Phoenician text, referring to the temple of Baalath, on a monument of Yehu-melek, its king (probably B.C. 600), has been discovered.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BACA , VALLEY OF (Psalm 84:6; R.V., “valley of weeping,” marg., “or balsam trees”), probably a valley in some part of Palestine, or generally some one of the valleys through which pilgrims had to pass on their way to the sanctuary of Jehovah on Zion; or it may be figuratively “a valley of weeping.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MULBERRY Hebrews bakah, “to weep;” rendered “Baca” (R.V., “weeping”) in Psalm 84:6. The plural form of the Hebrew bekaim is rendered “mulberry trees” in 2 Samuel 5:23, 24 and 1 Chronicles 14:14, 15. The tree here alluded to was probably the aspen or trembling poplar. “We know with certainty that the black poplar, the aspen, and the Lombardy poplar grew in Palestine. The aspen, whose long leaf-stalks cause the leaves to tremble with every breath of wind, unites with the willow and the oak to overshadow the watercourses of the Lebanon, and with the oleander and the acacia to adorn the ravines of Southern Palestine” (Kitto). By “the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees” we are to understand a rustling among the trees like the marching of an army. This was the signal that the Lord himself would lead forth David’s army to victory. (See SYCAMINE.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DOOR-KEEPER This word is used in Psalm 84:10 (R.V. marg., “stand at the threshold of,” etc.), but there it signifies properly “sitting at the threshold in the house of God.” The psalmist means that he would rather stand at the door of God’s house and merely look in, than dwell in houses where iniquity prevailed. Persons were appointed to keep the street door leading into the interior of the house (John 18:16, 17; Acts 12:13). Sometimes females held this post.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). RAHAB insolence; pride, a poetical name applied to Egypt in Psalm 87:4; 89:10; Isaiah 51:9, as “the proud one.” Rahab, (Hebrews Rahab; i.e., “broad,” “large”). When the Hebrews were encamped at Shittim, in the “Arabah” or Jordan valley opposite Jericho, ready to cross the river, Joshua, as a final preparation, sent out two spies to “spy the land.” After five days they returned, having swum across the river, which at this season, the month Abib, overflowed its banks from the melting of the snow on Lebanon. The spies reported how it had fared with them (Joshua 2:1-7). They had been exposed to danger in Jericho, and had been saved by the fidelity of Rahab the harlot, to whose house they had gone for protection. When the city of Jericho fell (6:17-25), Rahab and her whole family were preserved according to the promise of the spies, and were incorporated among the Jewish people. She afterwards became the wife of Salmon, a prince of the tribe of Judah (Ruth 4:21; 1 Chronicles 2:11; Matthew 1:5). “Rahab’s being asked to bring out the spies to the soldiers (Joshua 2:3) sent for them, is in strict keeping with Eastern manners, which would not permit any man to enter a woman’s house without her permission. The fact of her covering the spies with bundles of flax which lay on her house-roof (2:6) is an ‘undesigned coincidence’ which strictly corroborates the narrative. It was the time of the barley harvest, and flax and barley are ripe at the same time in the Jordan valley, so that the bundles of flax stalks might have been expected to be drying just then” (Geikie’s Hours, etc., ii., 390).

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Epistola ad Marcellinum §16 (c. 350 AD)

'O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee' (LXX 87:2) — Athanasius marks Ps 88 (LXX 87) as the AFFLICTION-PRAYER PARADIGM in the Letter to Marcellinus: prescribed for the soul-in-affliction-without-relief. Ps 88 is the darkest of the canonical Psalms (ending on darkness, not deliverance — phrasē mou aphēste philos kai plēsion kai tous gnōstous mou apo talaipōrias, 'thou hast put far from me lover and friend, and my acquaintances into darkness'). Athanasius's pastoral-counsel: the Psalter does not prescribe Ps 88 lightly; but for the soul-in-severe-affliction, even the dark-Psalm is Spirit-given consolation — the very-act-of-voicing-affliction-to-God IS the saving-prayer.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TABOR a height. (1.) Now Jebel et-Tur, a cone-like prominent mountain, 11 miles west of the Sea of Galilee. It is about 1,843 feet high. The view from the summit of it is said to be singularly extensive and grand. This is alluded to in Psalm 89:12; Jeremiah 46:18. It was here that Barak encamped before the battle with Sisera (q.v.) Judges 4:6-14. There is an old tradition, which, however, is unfounded, that it was the scene of the transfiguration of our Lord. (See HERMON.) “The prominence and isolation of Tabor, standing, as it does, on the border-land between the northern and southern tribes, between the mountains and the central plain, made it a place of note in all ages, and evidently led the psalmist to associate it with Hermon, the one emblematic of the south, the other of the north.” There are some who still hold that this was the scene of the transfiguration (q.v.). (2.) A town of Zebulum (1 Chronicles 6:77). (3.) The “plain of Tabor” (1 Samuel 10:3) should be, as in the Revised Version, “the oak of Tabor.” This was probably the Allon-bachuth of Genesis 35:8.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JUSTICE OF GOD that perfection of his nature whereby he is infinitely righteous in himself and in all he does, the righteousness of the divine nature exercised in his moral government. At first God imposes righteous laws on his creatures and executes them righteously. Justice is not an optional product of his will, but an unchangeable principle of his very nature. His legislative justice is his requiring of his rational creatures conformity in all respects to the moral law. His rectoral or distributive justice is his dealing with his accountable creatures according to the requirements of the law in rewarding or punishing them (Psalm 89:14). In remunerative justice he distributes rewards (James 1:12; 2 Timothy 4:8); in vindictive or punitive justice he inflicts punishment on account of transgression (2 Thessalonians 1:6). He cannot, as being infinitely righteous, do otherwise than regard and hate sin as intrinsically hateful and deserving of punishment. “He cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). His essential and eternal righteousness immutably determines him to visit every sin as such with merited punishment.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Epistola ad Marcellinum §20 (c. 350 AD)

'He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty' (LXX 90:1 — ho katoikōn en boētheia tou Hypsistou en skepē tou theou tou ouranou aulisthēsetai) — Athanasius marks Ps 91 (LXX 90) as the DIVINE-PROTECTION PARADIGM in the Letter to Marcellinus: prescribed for the soul-seeking-refuge-from-physical-and-spiritual-dangers. The shadow-of-the-Most-High (skepē tou Hypsistou) is read Christ-ologically — the Word-incarnate is the divine-shadow-cast-on-earth, the Annunciation-overshadowing (Lk 1:35 episkiasei soi) now-extended to every believer. The Tewahedo travel-blessing tradition cites Ps 91 as the Mäzmurä Dawit (David's Psalter) protective-prayer.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PALM TREE (Hebrews tamar), the date-palm characteristic of Palestine. It is described as “flourishing” (Psalm 92:12), tall (Cant. 7:7), “upright” (Jeremiah 10:5). Its branches are a symbol of victory (Revelation 7:9). “Rising with slender stem 40 or 50, at times even 80, feet aloft, its only branches, the feathery, snow-like, pale-green fronds from 6 to 12 feet long, bending from its top, the palm attracts the eye wherever it is seen.” The whole land of Palestine was called by the Greeks and Romans Phoenicia, i.e., “the land of palms.” Tadmor in the desert was called by the Greeks and Romans Palmyra, i.e., “the city of palms.” The finest specimens of this tree grew at Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3) and Engedi and along the banks of the Jordan. Branches of the palm tree were carried at the feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40). At our Lord’s triumphal entrance into Jerusalem the crowds took palm branches, and went forth to meet him, crying, “Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:8; John 12:13). (See DATE.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). POETRY has been well defined as “the measured language of emotion.” Hebrew poetry deals almost exclusively with the great question of man’s relation to God. “Guilt, condemnation, punishment, pardon, redemption, repentance are the awful themes of this heaven-born poetry.” In the Hebrew scriptures there are found three distinct kinds of poetry, (1) that of the Book of Job and the Song of Solomon, which is dramatic; (2) that of the Book of Psalms, which is lyrical; and (3) that of the Book of Ecclesiastes, which is didactic and sententious. Hebrew poetry has nothing akin to that of Western nations. It has neither metre nor rhyme. Its great peculiarity consists in the mutual correspondence of sentences or clauses, called parallelism, or “thought-rhyme.” Various kinds of this parallelism have been pointed out: (1.) Synonymous or cognate parallelism, where the same idea is repeated in the same words (Psalm 93:3; 94:1; Proverbs 6:2), or in different words (Psalm 22, 23, 28, 114, etc.); or where it is expressed in a positive form in the one clause and in a negative in the other (Psalm 40:12; Proverbs 6:26); or where the same idea is expressed in three successive clauses (Psalm 40:15, 16); or in a double parallelism, the first and second clauses corresponding to the third and fourth (Isaiah 9:1; 61:10, 11). (2.) Antithetic parallelism, where the idea of the second clause is the converse of that of the first (Psalm 20:8; 27:6, 7; 34:11; 37:9, 17, 21, 22). This is the common form of gnomic or proverbial poetry. (See Proverbs 10-15.) (3.) Synthetic or constructive or compound parallelism, where each clause or sentence contains some accessory idea enforcing the main idea (Psalm 19:7-10; 85:12; Job 3:3-9; Isaiah 1:5-9). (4.) Introverted parallelism, in which of four clauses the first answers to the fourth and the second to the third (Psalm 135:15-18; Proverbs 23:15, 16), or where the second line reverses the order of words in the first (Psalm 86:2). Hebrew poetry sometimes assumes other forms than these. (1.) An alphabetical arrangement is sometimes adopted for the purpose of connecting clauses or sentences. Thus in the following the initial words of the respective verses begin with the letters of the alphabet in regular succession: Proverbs 31:10-31; Lamentations 1, 2, 3, 4; Psalm 25, 34, 37, 145. Psalm 119 has a letter of the alphabet in regular order beginning every eighth verse. (2.) The repetition of the same verse or of some emphatic expression at intervals (Psalm 42, 107, where the refrain is in verses, 8, 15, 21, 31). (Comp. also Isaiah 9:8-10:4; Amos 1:3, 6, 9, 11, 13; 2:1, 4, 6.) (3.) Gradation, in which the thought of one verse is resumed in another (Psalm 121). Several odes of great poetical beauty are found in the historical books of the Old Testament, such as the song of Moses (Exodus 15), the song of Deborah (Judges 5), of Hannah (1 Samuel 2), of Hezekiah (Isaiah 38:9-20), of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3), and David’s “song of the bow” (2 Samuel 1:19-27).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DUMAH silence, (comp. Psalm 94:17), the fourth son of Ishmael; also the tribe descended from him; and hence also the region in Arabia which they inhabited (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). There was also a town of this name in Judah (Joshua 15:52), which has been identified with ed-Domeh, about 10 miles southwest of Hebron. The place mentioned in the “burden” of the prophet Isaiah (21:11) is Edom or Idumea.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Epistola ad Marcellinum §30 (c. 350 AD)

'Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee' (LXX 118:11 — en tē kardia mou ekrypsa ta logia sou hopōs an mē hamartō soi) — Athanasius marks Ps 119 (LXX 118) — the longest-Psalm, structured by the Hebrew-alphabet — as the WORD-INTERNALIZATION PARADIGM in the Letter to Marcellinus. The praying-soul does not merely-recite-the-word but HIDES-IT-IN-THE-HEART (ekrypsa en tē kardia) as protective-talisman-against-sin. The logia (oracles/divine-utterances) are Spirit-breathed-Scripture, and their-hiding-in-the-heart is the Spirit's-work-of-sanctifying-memory. Athanasius's pastoral-instruction: memorize the Psalter completely; the soul that knows-the-Psalter-by-heart has the Spirit's-prayer-vocabulary always-at-hand.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos II.13 (c. 350 AD)

'The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool' — Athanasius marks the dual-kyrios (eipen ho kyrios tō kyriō mou — 'YHWH said to my Adonai') as the canonical-OT prooftext for the eternal-distinction of Persons within the one-divine-Name. Christ's appeal to this verse at Mt 22:41-46 + Mk 12:35-37 + Lk 20:41-44 is what stops the Pharisaic objection cold: David himself in the Spirit calls his promised-Son 'Lord' — therefore the Messiah is more than David's biological-descendant; he is David's pre-existent divine-Lord. The 'sit at my right hand' is what Acts 2:34-35 + 1 Cor 15:25 + Eph 1:20 + Heb 1:13 cite as the post-resurrection enthronement fulfillment. Tewahedo Anaphora liturgy cites Ps 110:1 at the great-thanksgiving prefatory acclamation.

The Psalms 73:1.

A Psalm of Asaph. Truly God [is] good to Israel, [even] to such as are of a clean heart.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

מִזְמ֗וֹר לְאָ֫סָ֥ף אַ֤ךְ ט֭וֹב לְיִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל אֱלֹהִ֗ים לְבָרֵ֥י לֵבָֽב׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

Ψαλμὸς τῷ Ἀσάφ. Ὡς ἀγαθὸς τῷ Ἰσραὴλ ὁ θεός, τοῖς εὐθέσι τῇ καρδίᾳ.

Douay-Rheims

A psalm for Asaph. How good is God to Israel, to them that are of a right heart!

JPS (1917)

BOOK III A Psalm of Asaph. Surely God is good to Israel, even to such as are pure in heart.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Psalmus Asaph. [Quam bonus Israël Deus, his qui recto sunt corde !

Arabic (Van Dyck)

مَزْمُورٌ. لِآسَافَ إِنَّمَا صَالِحٌ ٱللهُ لِإِسْرَائِيلَ، لِأَنْقِيَاءِ ٱلْقَلْبِ.

↩

The Psalms 73:2.

But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וַאֲנִ֗י כִּ֭מְעַט נטוי רַגְלָ֑י כְּ֝אַ֗יִן שפכה אֲשֻׁרָֽי׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐμοῦ δὲ παρὰ μικρὸν ἐσαλεύθησαν οἱ πόδες, παρ᾽ ὀλίγον ἐξεχύθη τὰ διαβήματά μου.

Douay-Rheims

But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped.

JPS (1917)

But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Mei autem pene moti sunt pedes, pene effusi sunt gressus mei:

Arabic (Van Dyck)

أَمَّا أَنَا فَكَادَتْ تَزِلُّ قَدَمَايَ. لَوْلَا قَلِيلٌ لَزَلِقَتْ خَطَوَاتِي.

↩

The Psalms 73:3.

For I was envious at the foolish, [when] I saw the prosperity of the wicked.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

כִּֽי־קִ֭נֵּאתִי בַּֽהוֹלְלִ֑ים שְׁל֖וֹם רְשָׁעִ֣ים אֶרְאֶֽה׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὅτι ἐζήλωσα ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀνόμοις, εἰρήνην ἁμαρτωλῶν θεωρῶν·

Douay-Rheims

Because I had a zeal on occasion of the wicked, seeing the prosperity of sinners.

JPS (1917)

For I was envious at the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

quia zelavi super iniquos, pacem peccatorum videns.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

لِأَنِّي غِرْتُ مِنَ ٱلْمُتَكَبِّرِينَ، إِذْ رَأَيْتُ سَلَامَةَ ٱلْأَشْرَارِ.

↩

The Psalms 73:4.

For [there are] no bands in their death: but their strength [is] firm.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

כִּ֤י אֵ֖ין חַרְצֻבּ֥וֹת לְמוֹתָ֗ם וּבָרִ֥יא אוּלָֽם׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἀνάνευσις ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ αὐτῶν, καὶ στερέωμα ἐν τῇ μάστιγι αὐτῶν·

Douay-Rheims

For there is no regard to their death, nor is there strength in their stripes.

JPS (1917)

For there are no pangs at their death, and their body is sound.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Quia non est respectus morti eorum, et firmamentum in plaga eorum.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

لِأَنَّهُ لَيْسَتْ فِي مَوْتِهِمْ شَدَائِدُ، وَجِسْمُهُمْ سَمِينٌ.

↩

The Psalms 73:5.

They [are] not in trouble [as other] men; neither are they plagued like [other] men.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

בַּעֲמַ֣ל אֱנ֣וֹשׁ אֵינֵ֑מוֹ וְעִם־אָ֝דָ֗ם לֹ֣א יְנֻגָּֽעוּ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐν κόποις ἀνθρώπων οὐκ εἰσίν, καὶ μετὰ ἀνθρώπων οὐ μαστιγωθήσονται.

Douay-Rheims

They are not in the labour of men: neither shall they be scourged like other men.

JPS (1917)

In the trouble of man they are not; neither are they plagued like men.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

In labore hominum non sunt, et cum hominibus non flagellabuntur.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

لَيْسُوا فِي تَعَبِ ٱلنَّاسِ، وَمَعَ ٱلْبَشَرِ لَا يُصَابُونَ.

↩

The Psalms 73:6.

Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; violence covereth them [as] a garment.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

לָ֭כֵן עֲנָקַ֣תְמוֹ גַאֲוָ֑ה יַעֲטָף־שִׁ֝֗ית חָמָ֥ס לָֽמוֹ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

διὰ τοῦτο ἐκράτησεν αὐτοὺς ἡ ὑπερηφανία, περιεβάλοντο ἀδικίαν καὶ ἀσέβειαν αὐτῶν.

Douay-Rheims

Therefore pride hath held them fast: they are covered with their iniquity and their wickedness.

JPS (1917)

Therefore pride is as a chain about their neck; violence covereth them as a garment.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Ideo tenuit eos superbia; operti sunt iniquitate et impietate sua.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

لِذَلِكَ تَقَلَّدُوا ٱلْكِبْرِيَاءَ. لَبِسُوا كَثَوْبٍ ظُلْمَهُمْ.

↩

The Psalms 73:7.

Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

יָ֭צָא מֵחֵ֣לֶב עֵינֵ֑מוֹ עָ֝בְר֗וּ מַשְׂכִּיּ֥וֹת לֵבָֽב׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐξελεύσεται ὡς ἐκ στέατος ἡ ἀδικία αὐτῶν, διῆλθον εἰς διάθεσιν καρδίας·

Douay-Rheims

Their iniquity hath come forth, as it were from fatness: they have passed into the affection of the heart.

JPS (1917)

Their eyes stand forth from fatness; they are gone beyond the imaginations of their heart.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Prodiit quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum; transierunt in affectum cordis.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

جَحَظَتْ عُيُونُهُمْ مِنَ ٱلشَّحْمِ. جَاوَزُوا تَصَوُّرَاتِ ٱلْقَلْبِ.

↩

The Psalms 73:8.

They are corrupt, and speak wickedly [concerning] oppression: they speak loftily.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

יָמִ֤יקוּ ׀ וִידַבְּר֣וּ בְרָ֣ע עֹ֑שֶׁק מִמָּר֥וֹם יְדַבֵּֽרוּ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

διενοήθησαν καὶ ἐλάλησαν ἐν πονηρίᾳ, ἀδικίαν εἰς τὸ ὕψος ἐλάλησαν·

Douay-Rheims

They have thought and spoken wickedness: they have spoken iniquity on high.

JPS (1917)

They scoff, and in wickedness utter oppression; they speak as if there were none on high.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Cogitaverunt et locuti sunt nequitiam; iniquitatem in excelso locuti sunt.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ وَيَتَكَلَّمُونَ بِٱلشَّرِّ ظُلْمًا. مِنَ ٱلْعَلَاءِ يَتَكَلَّمُونَ.

↩

The Psalms 73:9.

They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

שַׁתּ֣וּ בַשָּׁמַ֣יִם פִּיהֶ֑ם וּ֝לְשׁוֹנָ֗ם תִּֽהֲלַ֥ךְ בָּאָֽרֶץ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἔθεντο εἰς οὐρανὸν τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν, καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα αὐτῶν διῆλθεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.

Douay-Rheims

They have set their mouth against heaven: and their tongue hath passed through the earth.

JPS (1917)

They have set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Posuerunt in cælum os suum, et lingua eorum transivit in terra.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

جَعَلُوا أَفْوَاهَهُمْ فِي ٱلسَّمَاءِ، وَأَلْسِنَتُهُمْ تَتَمَشَّى فِي ٱلْأَرْضِ.

↩

The Psalms 73:10.

Therefore his people return hither: and waters of a full [cup] are wrung out to them.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

לָכֵ֤ן ׀ ישיב עַמּ֣וֹ הֲלֹ֑ם וּמֵ֥י מָ֝לֵ֗א יִמָּ֥צוּ לָֽמוֹ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

διὰ τοῦτο ἐπιστρέψει ὁ λαός μου ἐνταῦθα, καὶ ἡμέραι πλήρεις εὑρεθήσονται αὐτοῖς,

Douay-Rheims

Therefore will my people return here and full days shall be found in them.

JPS (1917)

Therefore His people return hither; and waters of fullness are drained out by them.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Ideo convertetur populus meus hic, et dies pleni invenientur in eis.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

لِذَلِكَ يَرْجِعُ شَعْبُهُ إِلَى هُنَا، وَكَمِيَاهٍ مُرْوِيَةٍ يُمْتَصُّونَ مِنْهُمْ.

↩

The Psalms 73:11.

And they say, How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְֽאָמְר֗וּ אֵיכָ֥ה יָדַֽע־אֵ֑ל וְיֵ֖שׁ דֵּעָ֣ה בְעֶלְיֽוֹן׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καὶ εἶπαν Πῶς ἔγνω ὁ θεός; καὶ εἰ ἔστιν γνῶσις ἐν τῷ ὑψίστῳ;

Douay-Rheims

And they said: How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?

JPS (1917)

And they say: 'How doth God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?'

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Et dixerunt: Quomodo scit Deus, et si est scientia in excelso?

Arabic (Van Dyck)

وَقَالُوا: «كَيْفَ يَعْلَمُ ٱللهُ؟ وَهَلْ عِنْدَ ٱلْعَلِيِّ مَعْرِفَةٌ؟».

↩

The Psalms 73:12.

Behold, these [are] the ungodly, who prosper in the world; they increase [in] riches.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

הִנֵּה־אֵ֥לֶּה רְשָׁעִ֑ים וְשַׁלְוֵ֥י ע֝וֹלָ֗ם הִשְׂגּוּ־חָֽיִל׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἰδοὺ ἁμαρτωλοὶ καὶ εὐθηνοῦνται· εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατέσχον πλούτου.

Douay-Rheims

Behold these are sinners; and yet abounding in the world they have obtained riches.

JPS (1917)

Behold, such are the wicked; and they that are always at ease increase riches.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Ecce ipsi peccatores, et abundantes in sæculo obtinuerunt divitias.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

هُوَذَا هَؤُلَاءِ هُمُ ٱلْأَشْرَارُ، وَمُسْتَرِيحِينَ إِلَى ٱلدَّهْرِ يُكْثِرُونَ ثَرْوَةً.

↩

The Psalms 73:13.

Verily I have cleansed my heart [in] vain, and washed my hands in innocency.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

אַךְ־רִ֭יק זִכִּ֣יתִי לְבָבִ֑י וָאֶרְחַ֖ץ בְּנִקָּי֣וֹן כַּפָּֽי׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καὶ εἶπα Ἄρα ματαίως ἐδικαίωσα τὴν καρδίαν μου, καὶ ἐνιψάμην ἐν ἀθῴοις τὰς χεῖράς μου,

Douay-Rheims

And I said: Then have I in vain justified my heart, and washed my hands among the innocent.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

חָטָ֥אנוּ עִם־אֲבוֹתֵ֗ינוּ הֶעֱוִ֥ינוּ הִרְשָֽׁעְנוּ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἡμάρτομεν μετὰ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν, ἠνομήσαμεν, ἠδικήσαμεν·

Douay-Rheims

We have sinned with our fathers: we have acted unjustly, we have wrought iniquity.

JPS (1917)

We have sinned with our fathers, we have done iniquitously, we have dealt wickedly.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Peccavimus cum patribus nostris: injuste egimus; iniquitatem fecimus.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

أَخْطَأْنَا مَعَ آبَائِنَا. أَسَأْنَا وَأَذْنَبْنَا.

The Psalms 106:7.

Our fathers understood not thy wonders in Egypt; they remembered not the multitude of thy mercies; but provoked [him] at the sea, [even] at the Red sea.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

אֲב֘וֹתֵ֤ינוּ בְמִצְרַ֨יִם ׀ לֹא־הִשְׂכִּ֬ילוּ נִפְלְאוֹתֶ֗יךָ לֹ֣א זָ֭כְרוּ אֶת־רֹ֣ב חֲסָדֶ֑יךָ וַיַּמְר֖וּ עַל־יָ֣ם בְּיַם־סֽוּף׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ οὐ συνῆκαν τὰ θαυμάσιά σου, καὶ οὐκ ἐμνήσθησαν τοῦ πλήθους τοῦ ἐλέους σου, καὶ παρεπίκραναν ἀναβαίνοντες ἐν τῇ ἐρυθρᾷ θαλάσσῃ.

Douay-Rheims

Our fathers understood not thy wonders in Egypt: they remembered not the multitude of thy mercies: And they provoked to wrath going up to the sea, even the Red Sea.

JPS (1917)

Our fathers in Egypt gave no heed unto Thy wonders; they remembered not the multitude of Thy mercies; but were rebellious at the sea, even at the Red Sea.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Patres nostri in Ægypto non intellexerunt mirabilia tua; non fuerunt memores multitudinis misericordiæ tuæ. Et irritaverunt ascendentes in mare, mare Rubrum;

Arabic (Van Dyck)

آبَاؤُنَا فِي مِصْرَ لَمْ يَفْهَمُوا عَجَائِبَكَ. لَمْ يَذْكُرُوا كَثْرَةَ مَرَاحِمِكَ، فَتَمَرَّدُوا عِنْدَ ٱلْبَحْرِ، عِنْدَ بَحْرِ سُوفٍ.

Douay-Rheims

JPS (1917)

JPS (1917)
